tips.title: Smaller unit, bigger number
tips.body:
A metre is a big step, a centimetre a small one. The same length takes **more small steps** than big ones, so changing to a **smaller** unit makes the number **bigger**: multiply. To a **bigger** unit, divide.

3.5 m is 350 cm, not 0.035. Ask which unit is smaller before you touch the calculator.

tips.title: Square the step, cube the step
tips.body:
Picture a 1 m square tiled with centimetre squares: **100 rows of 100**, which is $10\,000$ of them, not 100.

Area units convert by the length factor **squared**; volume units by it **cubed**. So cm² to m² is **÷ $10\,000$** and cm³ to m³ is **÷ $1\,000\,000$**.

tips.title: Two units in one? Convert each
tips.body:
A compound unit such as **km/h** or **g/cm³** has a top unit and a bottom unit. Convert them **one at a time**: km to m on top, hours to seconds underneath.

Then divide. 72 km/h is 72 000 m in 3600 s, which is 20 m/s.

tips.title: Estimate before you press equals
tips.body:
Round every number to **1 significant figure** and work it out in your head. If the calculator answer is about **10 times** out from your estimate, look for a **decimal point** slip; if it is far out, look for **missing brackets**.

The estimate is what makes a calculator answer trustworthy.

tips.title: The 3.6 that turns km/h into m/s
tips.body:
There are 1000 m in a km and 3600 s in an hour, so 1 km/h is $\dfrac{1000}{3600} = \dfrac{1}{3.6}$ m/s.

**km/h ÷ 3.6 = m/s**, and **m/s × 3.6 = km/h**. The m/s number is always the **smaller** one.

why.matters:
A number with the wrong unit is not a slightly wrong answer; it is a different quantity. 3.5 metres and 3.5 centimetres differ by a factor of 100, and nothing in the digits warns you. Converting correctly, and knowing that an area or a volume converts by far more than a length does, is what lets a measurement mean the same thing to everyone who reads it.

Estimation is the other half of the same habit. A calculator is only as right as what was typed into it, and a one-line estimate done in your head is the check that catches a slipped decimal point or a missing bracket before it matters.

examples.title: The spacecraft lost to a unit
examples.body:
In 1999 NASA's **Mars Climate Orbiter** was lost as it arrived at Mars. A piece of ground software reported the push from the craft's small thruster firings in **pound-force seconds**; the navigation software that used those figures expected **newton-seconds**.

One pound-force is about **4.45 newtons**, so the navigation software took each push to be about 4.45 times weaker than it really was. The small errors added up over the months of the journey, and the orbiter passed far closer to the planet than planned.

No arithmetic was wrong. A number was passed on without its unit, and read in a different one.

bars.label: The push, as the software read it

props.caption: One pound-force second is about 4.45 newton-seconds.

visual.alt: Two bars to scale: the push the navigation software assumed, one unit long, and the push that really happened, about 4.45 times as long

examples.title: Tiling a floor
examples.body:
A kitchen floor is 3.5 m by 4 m, so its area is **14 m²**. The tiles are 50 cm by 50 cm, which is **2500 cm²** each.

To divide, the two areas need the **same unit**. Dividing by 100, as for a length, turns 2500 cm² into 25 m², and the floor then needs **0.56 of a tile**. Dividing by $10\,000$, as area needs, gives 0.25 m² per tile and **56 tiles**.

An estimate settles it before any calculating: a 50 cm tile is half a metre each way, so **4 tiles** cover a square metre, and 14 square metres need about $4 \times 14 = 56$.

visual.alt: A table comparing two conversions of a 2500 square centimetre tile: dividing by 100 gives 25 square metres and 0.56 tiles for the floor, while dividing by 10 000 gives 0.25 square metres and 56 tiles

examples.title: How far a car goes while the driver reacts
examples.body:
Speed limits are in km/h, but what happens in the moment before braking is measured in metres and seconds. Converting shows it.

50 km/h is $50\,000$ m in 3600 s, about **13.9 m every second**. Suppose a driver takes 1.5 seconds to react to a hazard. In that time the car travels about **20.8 m** before the brakes are even touched.

At 30 km/h the same 1.5 seconds covers **12.5 m**; at 70 km/h, about **29.2 m**. The distance grows in step with the speed, and a unit conversion is what turns a number on a sign into a length on the road.

props.caption: Distance travelled in 1.5 seconds, drawn to scale.

visual.alt: Three bars to scale showing the distance a car travels in 1.5 seconds: 12.5 metres at 30 kilometres per hour, 20.8 metres at 50 and 29.2 metres at 70

steps.title: The standard units, and which way to go
steps.body:
The metric units are built on **10, 100 and 1000**, so converting is one multiplication or one division. The only question is which.

- To a **smaller** unit, there are **more** of them: **multiply**. 3.5 kg is $3.5 \times 1000 = 3500$ g.
- To a **bigger** unit, there are **fewer**: **divide**. 450 cm is $450 \div 100 = 4.5$ m.

**Time is not decimal.** An hour has 60 minutes, not 100. A calculator answer of **2.4 hours** is 2 hours and $0.4 \times 60 = 24$ minutes: **2 hours 24 minutes**, not 2 hours 40.

**Money in decimals.** £4.5 on a calculator screen means **£4.50**; write money to two decimal places.

props.title: Multiply to go to the smaller unit

visuals.alt: A table of standard conversions: kilometres to metres times 1000, metres to centimetres times 100, centimetres to millimetres times 10, kilograms to grams times 1000, tonnes to kilograms times 1000, litres to millilitres times 1000, litres to centilitres times 100, hours to minutes times 60 and pounds to pence times 100

check.prompt: A calculator shows that a journey takes 2.4 hours. How long is that in hours and minutes?
check.solution: The 0.4 is a fraction of an **hour**, and an hour has 60 minutes: $0.4 \times 60 = 24$. So **2 hours 24 minutes**. Reading 0.4 as 40 minutes treats an hour as 100 minutes.

steps.title: Area units: square the factor
steps.body:
A metre is 100 cm, but a **square metre is not 100 cm²**. A square 1 m by 1 m is 100 cm by 100 cm, and its area is $100 \times 100 = 10\,000$ cm².

So for area, the length factor is **squared**:

- 1 cm² $= 10 \times 10 = 100$ mm²
- 1 m² $= 100 \times 100 = 10\,000$ cm²
- 1 km² $= 1000 \times 1000 = 1\,000\,000$ m²

The direction rule is unchanged: to a smaller unit, multiply; to a bigger one, divide.

**The trap.** 4500 cm² divided by 100 gives 45 m², which is 100 times too big. Divided by $10\,000$ it is **0.45 m²**, a bit less than half a square metre.

visuals.problem: Convert 3.5 m² to cm², and 4500 cm² to m².

steps.text: 1 m is 100 cm, so 1 m² is $100 \times 100 = 10\,000$ cm²
cm² is the **smaller** unit, so multiply: $3.5 \times 10\,000 = 35\,000$ cm²
m² is the **bigger** unit, so divide: $4500 \div 10\,000 = 0.45$ m²
Not $4500 \div 100 = 45$, which is 100 times too big
steps.note: the length factor used by mistake

steps.text: Sense check: 0.45 m² is a bit under half a square metre, and 4500 is a bit under half of $10\,000$

props.title: Square the step for area, cube it for volume

visuals.alt: A table showing that 1 metre is 100 centimetres, 1 square metre is 100 times 100, which is 10 000 square centimetres, and 1 cubic metre is 100 times 100 times 100, which is 1 000 000 cubic centimetres

check.solution: 1 m² is $100 \times 100 = 10\,000$ cm², so 2.5 m² is $2.5 \times 10\,000 = 25\,000$ cm². Multiplying by 100 uses the length factor; multiplying by $1\,000\,000$ uses the volume one.

steps.title: Volume and capacity: cube the factor
steps.body:
For volume the length factor is **cubed**: 1 m³ is $100 \times 100 \times 100 = 1\,000\,000$ cm³.

**Capacity** is how much a container holds, measured in litres and millilitres. The link to volume is worth knowing by heart:

- **1 cm³ = 1 ml**
- **1000 cm³ = 1 litre**
- **1 m³ = 1000 litres**

So a volume in cm³ becomes litres by dividing by 1000, and a volume in m³ becomes litres by multiplying by 1000.

visuals.alt: A cuboid fish tank 80 centimetres long, 40 centimetres wide and 50 centimetres high

visuals.problem: A fish tank is 80 cm long, 40 cm wide and 50 cm high. Find its volume in cm³, in litres and in m³.

steps.text: Volume $= 80 \times 40 \times 50 = 160\,000$ cm³
Litres: $1000$ cm³ is 1 litre, so $160\,000 \div 1000 = 160$ litres
Check another way: in metres the tank is $0.8 \times 0.4 \times 0.5 = 0.16$ m³
steps.note: converting the lengths first gives the same answer

steps.text: And $0.16$ m³ $\times 1000 = 160$ litres, which agrees

check.prompt: A water butt holds 0.6 m³. How many litres is that?
check.solution: 1 m³ is 1000 litres, so 0.6 m³ is $0.6 \times 1000 = 600$ litres.

steps.title: Compound units: convert the top and the bottom
steps.body:
A **compound unit** is made of two units, such as km/h (kilometres **per** hour), g/cm³ or £ per hour. The Year 10 topic on compound measures uses them in formulas; here the job is changing one into another.

The method: **convert the top unit, convert the bottom unit, then divide**.

- **km/h to m/s**: 72 km/h is $72\,000$ m in 3600 s, which is $72\,000 \div 3600 = 20$ m/s.
- **g/cm³ to kg/m³**: 2.7 g/cm³ means each cm³ has 2.7 g. A cubic metre holds $1\,000\,000$ cm³, so it has $2\,700\,000$ g, which is **2700 kg**: 2700 kg/m³.
- **£ per hour to pence per minute**: £12.60 an hour is 1260p in 60 minutes, which is **21p per minute**.
- **N/cm² to N/m²**: the bottom unit is an **area**, so its factor is squared. A square metre is $10\,000$ cm², so 2 N/cm² is **$20\,000$ N/m²**.

The g/cm³ result is worth remembering as a shortcut: **multiply by 1000**.

steps.text: Top unit: 72 km is $72 \times 1000 = 72\,000$ m
Bottom unit: 1 hour is $60 \times 60 = 3600$ s
Shortcut: $72 \div 3.6 = 20$
Sense check: m/s is the smaller number, because a second is so much shorter than an hour

visuals.alt: A table of compound unit conversions: kilometres per hour to metres per second is divide by 3.6, metres per second to kilometres per hour is times 3.6, grams per cubic centimetre to kilograms per cubic metre is times 1000, and pounds per hour to pence per minute is times 100 then divide by 60, and newtons per square centimetre to newtons per square metre is times 10 000

check.prompt: Convert a speed of 90 km/h to m/s.
check.solution: 90 km is $90\,000$ m and an hour is 3600 s, so the speed is $90\,000 \div 3600 = 25$ m/s. Or $90 \div 3.6 = 25$.

steps.title: Estimating: round to 1 significant figure
steps.body:
To **estimate** a calculation, round every number to **1 significant figure**, then work it out in your head.

The first significant figure is the first digit that is not zero. Keep that one, round it, and put zeros in to keep the size: 38.7 becomes 40, 851 becomes 900, 0.0462 becomes 0.05.

**Dividing by a decimal.** Rounding often leaves a divisor such as 0.2 or 0.5. Dividing by 0.2 is the same as **multiplying by 5**, because there are five 0.2s in every 1. Dividing by 0.5 doubles.

Write the estimate with the $\approx$ sign, which means *is approximately equal to*.

visuals.alt: A table of numbers rounded to 1 significant figure: 38.7 to 40, 5.12 to 5, 0.198 to 0.2, 0.0462 to 0.05, 851 to 900 and 2481 to 2000

steps.text: Round each number to 1 significant figure: 40, 5 and 0.2
Top: $40 \times 5 = 200$
Bottom: dividing by 0.2 is multiplying by 5
A calculator gives 1000.73 to 2 decimal places, so the estimate is close
steps.note: the point is the size, not the digits

check.prompt: Estimate the value of $\dfrac{6.8 \times 41.3}{0.52}$ by rounding each number to 1 significant figure.
check.solution: Rounded: $\dfrac{7 \times 40}{0.5} = \dfrac{280}{0.5} = 560$, because dividing by 0.5 doubles. 140 comes from multiplying by 0.5 instead of dividing, and 280 from leaving out the division.

steps.title: Checking a calculator answer
steps.body:
A calculator does exactly what it is told. If a bracket is left out or a decimal point is typed in the wrong place, it gives a wrong answer with complete confidence. An **estimate** is how you catch it.

- If the answer is about **10, 100 or 1000 times** bigger or smaller than the estimate, suspect a **decimal point** in the wrong place.
- If it is **far off** in some other way, suspect the **order of operations**: a fraction line needs brackets round its top or bottom when typed in one line.
- If it is **close** to the estimate, it is probably right.

The specification puts it as checking *answers obtained using technology*, and that is the habit: estimate first, calculate, then compare.

visuals.problem: Kate works out $\dfrac{23.4 + 17.9}{4.1}$ on a calculator and gets 27.77 to 2 decimal places. Is she right?

steps.text: Estimate: $\dfrac{20 + 20}{4} = 10$
Her answer, 27.77, is nearly three times the estimate, so something is wrong
She typed $23.4 + 17.9 \div 4.1$, which divides only the 17.9
With brackets, $(23.4 + 17.9) \div 4.1 = 10.07$ to 2 decimal places
That is close to the estimate of 10, so it can be trusted

visuals.alt: A table of what a comparison with the estimate suggests: about 10 times out suggests a decimal point slip, far out in another way suggests missed brackets, and close to it suggests the answer is probably right

check.prompt: Jay uses a calculator to work out 48.2 × 0.31 and writes down 149.42. Use an estimate to decide whether he is right.
check.solution: **No.** $50 \times 0.3 = 15$, and 149.42 is about ten times that, which points to a decimal point slip. The true value is $14.942$.
options: No: 50 × 0.3 = 15, so it is 10 times too big
Yes: 50 × 0.3 is 150, which is close to 149.42
Yes: an estimate cannot check a calculator
No: 48 × 3 = 144, so the answer must be 144

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**1.** Convert 5.6 km to metres.

**2.** Convert 3 m² to cm².

**3.** Convert 2500 cm³ to litres.

**4.** Convert 54 km/h to m/s.

**5.** Estimate $\dfrac{9.87 \times 3.14}{0.49}$.

Question 2 is the one to be careful with: an area, so the factor is squared.

visuals.alt: A table of answers to the five practice questions: 5600 metres, 30 000 square centimetres, 2.5 litres, 15 metres per second, and an estimate of 10 times 3 divided by 0.5, which is 60

check.solution: 1 m² is $10\,000$ cm², and m² is the bigger unit, so divide: $7500 \div 10\,000 = 0.75$ m².

steps.title: Going deeper: too big or too small, two steps, and letters
steps.body:
**Is the estimate too big or too small?** Look at which way each number was rounded.

- In a **product**, rounding numbers **up** makes the estimate too big: an **overestimate**. Rounding them all down gives an **underestimate**.
- In a **division**, the divisor works backwards. A **bigger** top or a **smaller** bottom makes the answer bigger. So rounding the top up and the bottom down gives an overestimate.
- If the roundings pull **both ways**, the direction cannot be read off. Work it out, or say so.

$3.6 \times 8.7 \approx 4 \times 9 = 36$ is an **overestimate**: both went up, and the true value is 31.32.

**Two-step conversions.** Chain the conversions one unit at a time, writing the unit at each step.

**Letters.** The specification also asks for conversions in *algebraic contexts*, and the factors work on letters just as on numbers. An area of $x$ m² is $10\,000x$ cm², and a speed of $v$ km/h is $\dfrac{v}{3.6} = \dfrac{5v}{18}$ m/s.

visuals.alt: A table of when an estimate is too big or too small: a product with both numbers rounded up is an overestimate and both down an underestimate; a division with the top rounded up and the bottom down is an overestimate and the reverse an underestimate; and mixed rounding must be worked out

visuals.problem: A steel beam has a volume of 0.05 m³. The density of the steel is 7.8 g/cm³. Find the mass of the beam in kg.

steps.text: The volume is in m³ and the density is per cm³, so change the density first
7.8 g/cm³ is $7.8 \times 1000 = 7800$ kg/m³
Mass $=$ density $\times$ volume $= 7800 \times 0.05 = 390$ kg
Check the size: a cubic metre of steel would be 7800 kg, and 0.05 m³ is a twentieth of that

check.prompt: Ben estimates 3.6 × 8.7 as 4 × 9 = 36. Is 36 an overestimate or an underestimate?
check.solution: Both 3.6 and 8.7 were rounded **up**, so their product grew: 36 is an **overestimate**. The true value is 31.32.
options: Overestimate: both numbers were rounded up
Exact: rounding to 1 s.f. keeps the answer
It cannot be told without working it out

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **To a smaller unit, multiply; to a bigger unit, divide.** The metric factors are 10, 100 and 1000.
- **Time is not decimal**: 0.4 hours is $0.4 \times 60 = 24$ minutes.
- **Money** is written to two decimal places: £4.50, not £4.5.
- **Area**: square the length factor. 1 m² $= 10\,000$ cm².
- **Volume**: cube it. 1 m³ $= 1\,000\,000$ cm³.
- **Capacity**: 1 cm³ = 1 ml, 1000 cm³ = 1 litre, 1 m³ = 1000 litres.
- **Compound units**: convert the top, convert the bottom, then divide.
- **km/h ÷ 3.6 = m/s**, and g/cm³ × 1000 = kg/m³.
- **Estimate** by rounding every number to 1 significant figure.
- Dividing by 0.2 is multiplying by 5; dividing by 0.5 doubles.
- **Check a calculator** against the estimate: 10 times out suggests a decimal slip, far out suggests brackets.
- **Over or under**: in a product, rounding up overestimates; in a division, a smaller divisor overestimates.

visuals.alt: Four boxes around units and estimates: the direction of a conversion, squaring and cubing the factor for area and volume, converting both parts of a compound unit, and estimating to 1 significant figure to check a calculator

check.prompt: How many cm³ are there in 1 m³?
check.solution: 1 m is 100 cm, so 1 m³ is $100 \times 100 \times 100 = 1\,000\,000$ cm³. $10\,000$ is the number of cm² in 1 m², and 1000 is the number of litres in 1 m³.

questions.prompt: Convert 2.75 km to metres.
questions.solution: A metre is smaller, so multiply: $2.75 \times 1000 = 2750$ m.

questions.prompt: Convert 450 cm to metres.
questions.solution: A metre is bigger, so divide: $450 \div 100 = 4.5$ m.

questions.prompt: How many square centimetres are there in 1 square metre?
questions.solution: A square metre is 100 cm by 100 cm, so it is $100 \times 100 = 10\,000$ cm². 100 is the number of cm in a metre, and $1\,000\,000$ is the number of cm³ in a m³.

questions.prompt: Convert 1.25 litres to millilitres.
questions.solution: There are 1000 ml in a litre: $1.25 \times 1000 = 1250$ ml.

questions.prompt: Estimate 4.87 × 21.3 by rounding each number to 1 significant figure.
questions.solution: 4.87 rounds to 5 and 21.3 to 20, so $5 \times 20 = 100$. 80 comes from cutting 4.87 down to 4 instead of rounding it, and 103.731 is the exact answer, not an estimate.

questions.prompt: A film lasts 1.6 hours. How many minutes is that?
questions.solution: An hour is 60 minutes, so $1.6 \times 60 = 96$ minutes (1 hour 36 minutes, not 1 hour 60 minutes).

questions.prompt: Convert 6800 cm² to m².
questions.solution: 1 m² is $100 \times 100 = 10\,000$ cm², and m² is the bigger unit, so divide: $6800 \div 10\,000 = 0.68$ m².

questions.prompt: A tank holds 0.3 m³ of water. How many litres is that?
questions.solution: 1 m³ is 1000 litres, so $0.3 \times 1000 = 300$ litres.

questions.prompt: A train travels at 108 km/h. What is this speed in m/s?
A plastic has a density of 1.3 g/cm³. What is its density in kg/m³?
questions.solution: A cubic metre holds $1\,000\,000$ cm³, so it has $1.3 \times 1\,000\,000 = 1\,300\,000$ g, which is $1\,300\,000 \div 1000 = 1300$ kg. So 1300 kg/m³.

markScheme.description: multiplies by 1 000 000 and divides by 1000, or multiplies by 1000

questions.prompt: Estimate the value of $\dfrac{61.8 \times 3.9}{0.21}$ by rounding each number to 1 significant figure.
questions.solution: Rounded: $\dfrac{60 \times 4}{0.2} = \dfrac{240}{0.2} = 1200$, because dividing by 0.2 multiplies by 5. 48 comes from multiplying by 0.2, 240 from leaving out the division, and $12\,000$ from dividing by 0.02.

questions.prompt: A fish tank is a cuboid 60 cm long, 40 cm wide and 25 cm high. How many litres of water does it hold when full?
questions.solution: Volume $= 60 \times 40 \times 25 = 60\,000$ cm³. There are 1000 cm³ in a litre, so it holds $60\,000 \div 1000 = 60$ litres.

questions.prompt: Sara is paid £11.40 an hour. How much is that per minute?
questions.solution: £11.40 is 1140p, and an hour is 60 minutes: $1140 \div 60 = 19$p per minute. £0.19 is right in pounds, but written as 0.19p it is a hundred times too small.

questions.prompt: A tap delivers water at 12 litres per minute. What is this rate in cm³ per second?
questions.solution: 12 litres is $12 \times 1000 = 12\,000$ cm³, and a minute is 60 s. So the rate is $12\,000 \div 60 = 200$ cm³ per second.

questions.prompt: A garden pond holds 1.2 m³ of water. A hose fills it at 8 litres per minute. How many hours does it take to fill the empty pond?
questions.solution: 1.2 m³ is $1.2 \times 1000 = 1200$ litres. At 8 litres a minute that takes $1200 \div 8 = 150$ minutes, which is $150 \div 60 = 2.5$ hours.

questions.prompt: A metal bar has a volume of 0.02 m³. The metal has a density of 8.9 g/cm³. Find the mass of the bar in kg.
questions.solution: Change the density to match the volume: 8.9 g/cm³ is $8.9 \times 1000 = 8900$ kg/m³. Mass $= 8900 \times 0.02 = 178$ kg.

questions.prompt: A cheetah is timed running at 30 m/s. A car is travelling at 100 km/h. How many km/h faster than the car is the cheetah?
questions.solution: Put both in km/h: $30 \times 3.6 = 108$ km/h. The cheetah is $108 - 100 = 8$ km/h faster.

questions.prompt: To estimate 47.6 ÷ 5.3, Kai rounds each number to 1 significant figure and works out 50 ÷ 5 = 10. Is 10 an overestimate or an underestimate?
questions.solution: A bigger top and a smaller bottom both make a division **bigger**, so 10 is an **overestimate**. The true value is 8.98 to 2 decimal places.
options: Overestimate: a bigger top, a smaller bottom
Neither: an estimate cannot be over or under

questions.prompt: Mia says: "1 m is 100 cm, so 5 m² is 500 cm²." Which is the best response?
questions.solution: **Wrong.** A square metre is 100 cm by 100 cm, which is $10\,000$ cm², so 5 m² is $50\,000$ cm². Mia has used the length factor for an area.
options: Right: area units convert in just the same way as lengths
Right: 1 m is 100 cm, so multiply by 100
Wrong: 1 m² is 1000 cm², so 5 m² is 5000 cm²
Wrong: 1 m² is $10\,000$ cm², so 5 m² is $50\,000$ cm²

questions.prompt: A square has sides of length $x$ metres. Which expression gives its area in cm²?
questions.solution: Each side is $100x$ cm, so the area is $(100x)^2 = 10\,000x^2$ cm². $100x^2$ squares the $x$ but not the 100, and dividing by $10\,000$ goes the wrong way, since cm² is the smaller unit.

questions.prompt: Water flows along a pipe at 0.5 m/s. The area of the cross-section of the pipe is 20 cm². How many litres of water flow out of the pipe each minute?
questions.solution: 0.5 m/s is 50 cm/s, so each second a column of water 50 cm long and 20 cm² in cross-section comes out: $50 \times 20 = 1000$ cm³, which is 1 litre. In a minute that is $1 \times 60 = 60$ litres.

questions.prompt: A builder is ordering concrete for a slab 4.9 m long, 3.1 m wide and 0.18 m deep. He estimates the volume as 5 × 3 × 0.2 = 3 m³ and says: "I rounded, so 3 m³ is definitely enough." Evaluate his statement.
questions.solution:
The builder rounded 4.9 up to 5 and 0.18 up to 0.2, but he rounded 3.1 **down** to 3. When the roundings pull in different directions there is no guarantee that the estimate is bigger than the true value, so his reason does not work.

The true volume is $4.9 \times 3.1 \times 0.18 = 2.7342$ m³, which is 2.73 m³ to 2 decimal places. That is less than 3 m³, so for this slab 3 m³ is enough, but only because the numbers happen to work out.

A slab 5.4 m by 3.4 m by 0.24 m rounds to exactly the same estimate, 5 × 3 × 0.2 = 3 m³, yet needs 4.41 m³. Rounding by itself does not make an estimate enough. To be sure of ordering enough, he should round every length **up**, which gives an overestimate.

questions.prompt: Show that a speed of 45 km/h is 12.5 m/s. Hence find how far, in metres, a car travelling at 45 km/h goes in 4 seconds.
questions.solution:
45 km is $45 \times 1000 = 45\,000$ m, and 1 hour is $60 \times 60 = 3600$ s. So 45 km/h is $45\,000 \div 3600 = 12.5$ m/s, as required.

In 4 seconds the car travels $12.5 \times 4 = 50$ m.

In 4 seconds the car travels $12.5 \times 4 = 50$ m.

questions.prompt: A crate presses on the floor with a pressure of 3 N/cm². What is this pressure in N/m²?
questions.solution: The bottom unit is an area. 1 m² is $100 \times 100 = 10\,000$ cm², so a square metre carries $10\,000$ times the force on one square centimetre: $3 \times 10\,000 = 30\,000$ N/m². A square metre is bigger, so the number per m² must be bigger.

examTechnique.body:
Before converting, decide which unit is smaller. Changing to a smaller unit makes the number bigger, so multiply; changing to a bigger unit makes it smaller, so divide. Write the unit beside every number in the working, so a wrong direction shows up as a wrong-looking number.

For an area, square the length factor; for a volume, cube it. A common slip is dividing cm² by 100 to get m².

For a compound unit, convert the top and the bottom separately, then divide, and keep the unit written at each step. In a problem that mixes units, such as a density per cm³ and a volume in m³, change one of them so they match before multiplying.

When a question says *estimate*, show the rounded numbers. Round each to 1 significant figure unless told otherwise, and write the calculation with those values, so the method can be seen.

If asked whether an estimate is too big or too small, say which way each number was rounded and what that does. Remember that in a division the bottom number works in reverse.

In a calculator question, estimate as well. It takes seconds, and an answer 10 times out from the estimate is often a decimal point in the wrong place.
examinerErrors: Dividing by 100 to change cm² to m², instead of by 10 000.
Dividing by 1000 to change cm³ to m³, instead of by 1 000 000.
Multiplying when changing to a bigger unit, so 450 cm becomes 45 000 m.
Converting only one part of a compound unit, such as the kilometres but not the hours.
Estimating by working out the exact answer and then rounding it, instead of rounding first.
Multiplying by 0.2 when the estimate divides by 0.2.
Calling an estimate an overestimate because one number was rounded up, without looking at the others.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer writes the unit at every step, so the direction of each conversion is visible and checkable. It squares the length factor for area and cubes it for volume without being prompted, and treats a compound unit as two conversions and a division. It converts one quantity to match another before combining them, and it can carry the same factors through a letter, writing an area of x square metres as 10 000x square centimetres. Its estimates show the rounded values, deal with division by a decimal cleanly, and say which way each number was rounded before deciding whether the estimate is too big or too small, including when the roundings pull both ways and the only honest answer is to work it out.
